facts.text: Etowah began as a lumber camp for the Chapman and Dewey Lumber Company in the 1890s, drawing workers to the swampy Mississippi Delta.
In 1902 a post office opened, and the name 'Etowah'—chosen after other options were rejected—stayed with the town.
The arrival of the Jonesboro, Lake City and Eastern Railroad that same year linked Etowah to Big Lake and Blytheville, boosting timber and crop transport.
Before European settlement, Native Americans built mounds and villages across Etowah’s swampy cypress forests, leaving archaeological traces that echo the region’s prehistoric culture.
Drainage projects in the late 19th and early 20th centuries turned Etowah’s marshlands into fertile farmland, supporting crops like cotton, soybeans, and rice.
The Little River’s Left Hand Chute slices through Etowah’s southeastern corner, a reminder of the town’s riverine geography.
